claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is governed by competition between configurational entropy and Al-driven local chemical ordering.
Strong interactions between Al and Co promote B2-type chemical ordering.
Strong interactions between Al and Ni promote B2-type chemical ordering.
Al-driven ordering nucleates B2-type ordered nanoscale precipitates within a disordered FCC matrix.
The spatial distribution and volume fraction of B2 precipitates determine retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni produced by casting and homogenization initially has a predominantly disordered FCC structure.
Varying Al content by approximately ±5 atomic percentage points under identical aging conditions provides a controlled test of Al-induced ordering.
B2-like precipitates alter local lattice distortions.
B2-like precipitates alter interphase energies.
Precipitate-induced changes in lattice distortion and interphase energy affect dislocation motion and defect resistance.
Increasing Al content allows specific Al–Co and Al–Ni interactions to overcome entropy stabilization and induce local ordering.
An optimal dispersion of B2 precipitates strengthens the matrix at high temperature.
An optimal dispersion of B2 precipitates improves environmental resistance.
Coherent B2–FCC interfaces help preserve radiation tolerance.
Coherent B2–FCC interfaces help preserve cryogenic toughness.
Lower-Al alloys with little ordering remain entirely disordered FCC, favoring toughness but reducing high-temperature strength.
Moderately increasing Al relative to the baseline will increase B2 ordering detectable by XRD and TEM.
Moderately increasing Al and B2 ordering will increase high-temperature strength and environmental resistance relative to the baseline.
Excessive B2 precipitate volume fraction or coarsening will reduce cryogenic toughness.
Failure of Al variation to change B2 ordering systematically, or failure of measured properties to correlate with ordering as predicted, would reject the hypothesis.
